read.sections.0.heading.source: A building people keep working on
read.sections.0.heading.back: A building people keep looking after

read.sections.0.text.source:
A building can last for generations because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different kinds of care. Some materials need regular renewal, so keeping a place does not always mean leaving every surface untouched. Conservation is care that helps valued heritage last. It means understanding what matters about a building, and how its material, use and meaning can continue.

The Great Mosque of Djenné stands in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO names the Old Towns of Djenné as an important example of earthen architecture: building with materials made from earth. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907. That date matters. The building we see is connected with a longer religious and urban history. But its present structure should not simply be described as unchanged since medieval times.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A building can last for several generations because people keep looking after it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different kinds of care. Some materials need to be renewed regularly, so looking after a place does not always mean leaving every surface untouched. Conservation is care that helps valued heritage last long. Conservation means understanding what is important about a building, and how its material, use and meaning can continue.

The Great Mosque of Djenné stands in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO names the Old Towns of Djenné as an important example of earthen architecture, that is, building with materials made from earth. The mosque there now was rebuilt in 1906–1907. That date matters. The building we see is connected with a longer religious and urban history. But its present structure should not simply be described as unchanged since the Middle Ages.
read.sections.0.text.note: "conservation" is "pemuliharaan" and "restoration" is "pemulihan", as Southeast Asia's TERMS (Lesson 11).

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A building can last a long time because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different care. Some materials must be renewed often. So keeping a place does not always mean leaving it untouched. Conservation is care that helps a valued place last. It means knowing what matters about a building, and how to keep it going.

The Great Mosque of Djenné is in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO calls Djenné's old towns a key example of earthen architecture. That means buildings made with earth. The mosque we see now was rebuilt in 1906 and 1907. The town's history is much older. We should not say it is unchanged since long ago.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
A building can last long because people keep looking after it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different care. Some materials must often be renewed. So looking after a place does not always mean leaving it untouched. Conservation is care that helps a valued place last long. It means we know what is important about a building, and how to keep it.

The Great Mosque of Djenné is in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO calls Djenné's old towns a main example of earthen architecture. That means buildings made with earth. The mosque we see now was rebuilt in 1906 and 1907. The town's history is much older. We should not say the mosque has not changed since long ago.
read.sections.0.simpler.note: "selalu" here means "often", the Malaysian sense, which is what the English means ("renewed often").

read.sections.1.text.source:
The town's wider setting explains why this mosque mattered. Djenné grew as a market centre connected with the trans-Saharan gold trade, the trade in gold across the Sahara Desert. It became important for the spread of Islam in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Waterways also linked the town with other trading places. Trade, religious learning and local building knowledge belonged to the same urban history. Islamic identity did not require copying one form of building used everywhere. People used regional materials and skills to make a place of worship suited to their setting.

Earth is a skilled building material here. UNESCO's Urban Heritage Atlas describes sun-baked earth bricks coated with mud plaster. The wooden pieces that stick out from the walls, and the shaped surfaces, give the mosque a distinctive look. The photographs in this lesson show parts of the outside in 2005. They record what was visible then; they do not show the building's condition today.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The town's wider setting explains why this mosque matters. Djenné grew as a market centre connected with the trans-Saharan gold trade, that is, the trade in gold across the Sahara Desert. The town became important in the spread of Islam in the 15th and 16th centuries. Waterways also connected the town with other trading places. Trade, religious learning and local building knowledge belong to the same urban history. Islamic identity did not require copying one form of building used everywhere. People used regional materials and skills to make a place of worship suited to their setting.

Earth is a building material that needs skill here. UNESCO's Urban Heritage Atlas describes earth bricks dried in the sun and coated with mud plaster. The pieces of wood that stick out from the walls, and the shaped surfaces, give the mosque a distinctive look. The photos in this lesson show part of its outside in 2005. These photos record what was visible at that time; these photos do not show the building's condition today.

Waterways, such as rivers, linked it to other trading towns. Trade, religious learning and building skills grew up together there. Muslims did not have to copy one style of building. People here used local materials and skills. They made a mosque that suits its place.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Care, knowledge and the people of Djenné
read.sections.2.heading.back: Care, knowledge and the people of Djenné

read.sections.2.text.source:
Looking after earthen buildings depends on knowledge and cooperation. The atlas describes Djenné's masons, the skilled builders, and how building skills are passed on. It also names the yearly plastering of the mosque as a practice that connects two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the physical building. Intangible heritage is the knowledge, organisation and shared practices around it. People take part in the life of the place through work as well as worship.

Regular care does not prevent every problem. A UNESCO report from December 2009 describes extra restoration and strengthening work involving traditional masons. Restoration is work to recover or make clearer an earlier form or condition. This dated report shows that yearly surface care and specialist repairs to the structure are different kinds of work. It should not be read as a current report of an emergency still going on.

Djenné is also a town where people live, trade and learn, and want comfortable homes and public services. Conservation needs to consider those lives. Treating a place only as attractive scenery can leave out the people whose knowledge keeps it going. A careful account asks which features carry historical and cultural meaning, and how they are looked after. It also asks how decisions involve the communities who use them.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Looking after earthen buildings depends on knowledge and cooperation. The atlas describes Djenné's masons, that is, skilled builders, and how building skills are passed down. The atlas also names the plastering of the mosque every year as a practice that connects two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the physical building. Intangible heritage is the knowledge, organisation and shared practices around it. People take part in the life of the place through work as well as worship.

Regular care does not prevent every problem. A UNESCO report from December 2009 describes extra restoration and strengthening work involving traditional masons. Restoration is work to bring back or make clearer an earlier form or condition. This dated report shows that care of the surface every year and repairs to the structure by specialists are different kinds of work. This report should not be read as a current report of an emergency that is still happening.

Djenné is also a town where people live, trade and learn, and they want comfortable homes and public services. Conservation needs to take those lives into account. Treating a place only as beautiful scenery can leave out the people whose knowledge keeps the place going. A careful account asks which features carry historical and cultural meaning, and how those features are looked after. That account also asks how decisions involve the communities who use them.
read.sections.2.text.note: "tangible / intangible heritage" are "warisan ketara / warisan tidak ketara", the terms Malaysia's Jabatan Warisan Negara uses. "masons" are "tukang bina".

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Caring for earth buildings takes skill and teamwork. Djenné's masons are skilled builders. They pass their skills on to others. Every year, people put new plaster on the mosque. This links two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the building itself. Intangible heritage is the knowledge and shared ways of doing things. People help the mosque through work as well as worship.

Yearly care cannot stop every problem. In December 2009, a UNESCO report told of extra repairs. Masons who use old skills did the work. Restoration is work to bring back an earlier form or condition. So the yearly plaster and big repairs are different jobs. That report is from 2009. It does not describe a problem today.

People also live, trade and learn in Djenné. They want good homes and services. Conservation must think about their lives too. A place is not just a pretty view. The people who keep it going matter. Good choices include the people who use the place.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Looking after earth buildings needs skill and teamwork. Djenné's masons are skilled builders. They pass their skills down to other people. Every year, people plaster the mosque with new plaster. This connects two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the building itself. Intangible heritage is knowledge and shared ways of doing things. People help the mosque through work as well as worship.

Care every year cannot stop all problems. In December 2009, a UNESCO report told of extra repairs. Masons who use old skills did that work. Restoration is work to bring back an earlier form or condition. So the plaster every year and big repairs are different jobs. That report is from 2009. That report does not describe a problem today.

People also live, trade and learn in Djenné. They want good homes and services. Conservation must think about their lives too. A place is not just a beautiful view. The people who keep it going matter. Good choices involve the people who use the place.

write.prompt.source: Explain why caring for the mosque needs both materials and people's knowledge. Use one detail of each from the reading.
write.prompt.back: Explain why caring for the mosque needs materials as well as people's knowledge. Use one detail of each from the reading.

write.example.source: The mosque is made of earth bricks and mud plaster. This material needs care again and again, so people put new plaster on the mosque every year. People's knowledge matters too. Djenné's masons know how to do this work, and they pass their skills on to others. The building lasts because of both its earth and the people who look after it.
write.example.back: The mosque is made of earth bricks and mud plaster. This material needs care again and again, so people plaster the mosque with new plaster every year. People's knowledge is also important. Djenné's masons know how to do this work, and they pass their skills down to other people. The building lasts because of its earth and also the people who look after it.

educatorNotes.0.source: Misconception to watch for: authentic heritage must never change, or building with earth shows a lack of skill. Both hide the documented techniques and the continuing social life of Djenné.
educatorNotes.0.back: Misconception to watch for: that authentic heritage must never change at all, or that building with earth shows a lack of skill. Both hide the documented techniques and the continuing social life of Djenné.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: earth bricks and mud plaster need suitable, regular care; masons and community practices keep the knowledge and the organised work going. Regular renewal can sustain a heritage place, while particular restoration decisions still need evidence. Simple English is fine.

Regular renewal can sustain a heritage place, while particular restoration decisions still need evidence. Simple language is enough.

educatorNotes.4.source: Don't merge the present town and mosque with the older archaeological site of Djenné-Djeno, or with the borders of a single medieval empire. The trade, Islam and waterway context comes from the UNESCO site record and the atlas.
